title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
items.content_text: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. This stays the lead five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and The Register; Minnesota impact detail from state officials and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued 30 Jul 2026 — re-verified 3 Sep 2026, 6:19 PM ET

items.title: Attackers walked from a wind farm’s firewall to another plant’s PLCs across a shared cellular APN — and stopped a turbine
items.content_text: CERT Polska’s follow-up report on attacks against Poland’s energy sector documents an intrusion path that maps almost exactly onto the exposure CISA and the NCSC are now warning about, and it is the reason this older item belongs on the page. Attackers compromised a FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, moved to a Teltonika cellular router, and then crossed a private cellular APN that had been provisioned without client isolation — meaning every SIM on that APN could reach every other. On the far side sat a WAGO PFC200 at a separate combined heat and power plant, still carrying default administrator credentials, which the attackers used to build an SSH bridge into the OT network. From there they forced three Siemens PLCs into STOP and set password protection on them, shutting down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment serving a town of roughly 50,000 people. CERT Polska assesses this as the first documented real-world OT intrusion via lateral movement across a private APN, and notes the shared-APN-without-isolation configuration is common in Poland and likely well beyond it.
tags: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, energy; first documented private-APN pivot

items.title: A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
items.content_text: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable.
tags: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)

items.title: A water-sector PLC maker was ransomed, and roughly 200 of its SCADA systems are reachable from the internet
items.content_text: Micro-Comm of Olathe, Kansas — which builds programmable logic controllers and the SCADAview CSX platform used by water and wastewater utilities — discovered a breach on 31 July and confirmed it publicly on 26 August, with the FBI investigating. The Barracuda ransomware group, a profit-motivated crew that says it is not state sponsored, published what it claims are nearly 850,000 stolen files totalling about 644 GB. Researchers reviewing the file listing report references to municipal customers, a US military facility, employee names and product documentation including system diagrams. The FBI has told the company it assesses the intrusion as opportunistic rather than targeted, and no manipulation of any customer’s control system has been reported. The number that should hold a water operator’s attention is a separate one: roughly 200 SCADAview CSX systems across US states are reachable from the public internet — the same exposure pattern that carried July’s campaign into more than 100 water systems.

items.title: Day nine at Boston Scientific: plants still disrupted by a breach that never reached a controller
items.content_text: Nine days after detecting an intrusion on 25 August, Boston Scientific still has no full restoration date. Manufacturing, order processing and global shipping remain disrupted, with EDI and GHX orders queuing unfulfilled. The company’s 30 August update states that investigators have found no signs of malicious activity in its environment since detection, that the unauthorised access appears confined to certain on-premise systems rather than cloud, and that it hoped to resume shipping at least some products this week. CrowdStrike and other responders remain engaged. Implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring are unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware involvement has been named, and no group has credibly claimed it. For OT defenders the lesson is unchanged and getting louder: an enterprise-side compromise that never touched a PLC has now disrupted production for the better part of a fortnight.
tags: Boston Scientific — Confirmed IT incident, production disrupted

items.title: NCSC: OT targeting is up across sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published a statement on 27 August saying it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors worldwide, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The agency ties it to a broader pattern of disruptive activity against internet-exposed systems and edge devices — routers, gateways and firewalls that hand an attacker a foothold. Its asks are concrete: keep an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems, understand what each edge device does and where its data flows, patch promptly, retire end-of-life equipment, disable Telnet and SNMP v1/v2, and watch for unexpected configuration changes or outbound connections. Coming a day after CISA’s exposure guidance, this is two national agencies independently reaching the same conclusion in the same week.
tags: Agency warning — Cross-sector OT targeting, real-world disruption

items.title: A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC.
tags: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs

items.title: The Five Eyes isolation guidance, reduced to six steps — and the hard one is running islanded for three months
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a working read of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance on 2 September, condensing the July joint publication into six sequential steps: identify the vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and map every connection; pre-build the separation points before you need them; write and test graduated isolation plans; keep visibility while isolated; and run a defined set of post-isolation checks before reconnecting. The step operators keep stumbling on is the planning assumption underneath: the guidance expects you to be able to sustain isolated operation for up to three months, not for an afternoon. That reframes isolation from an incident-response button into a design constraint, because a three-month island needs local authentication, local historian and licence servers, on-site spares, paper procedures and a supply of consumables ordered without the ERP that normally orders them. This is preparedness advice rather than a response to any new threat, but it lands against a month of confirmed OT disruption, which is why it is being read now.

items.title: Fire Ant moved up a layer: the routers and TACACS servers your OT quietly trusts are now the objective
items.content_text: Sygnia published incident-response findings on 31 August showing that the espionage actor it tracks as Fire Ant — assessed as substantially mirroring the China-nexus cluster reported elsewhere as UNC3886 — has expanded beyond hypervisor compromise into what the firm calls the trusted infrastructure layer. In the intrusions Sygnia investigated, the actor compromised Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts, then used them as operating platforms for traffic collection, credential theft and long-term persistence, explicitly in order to reach connected high-value environments including critical infrastructure. The tooling included Medusa rootkit components, custom SSH backdoors, malware masquerading as Zabbix monitoring agents and packet-triggered backdoors, some dating to 2025 and reused this year. The detail OT teams should sit with is the anti-forensics: the actor suppressed router logging, altered command output so operators saw a clean device, and tampered with host logs, meaning no single telemetry source could reconstruct the intrusion. No manipulation of a physical process has been reported — this is pre-positioning in the control plane that OT depends on.
tags: Threat research — Sygnia; China-nexus actor targeting network and authentication infrastructure

items.title: 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter — and not one attacker touched a control system
items.content_text: Dragos’ analysis of publicly disclosed victims and leak-site postings for the second quarter of 2026, published 11 August, counts 1,140 ransomware incidents affecting industrial organisations worldwide, up roughly 12% on the 1,020 recorded in the first quarter. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them, about 65% of the total, with construction at 176, equipment manufacturing at 114 and food and beverage at 70. The finding that matters operationally is the negative one: Dragos observed no case in the quarter in which a ransomware operator reached Stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain or manipulated a control system directly. Where production stopped, it stopped because the enterprise systems that operations depend on — ERP, MES, virtualisation, identity — were encrypted, or because the operator shut the plant down precautionarily. The tradecraft stayed consistent: exploitation of internet-facing edge devices and remote management tooling, abuse of valid accounts, credential theft, EDR-killer utilities and bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver techniques, with a continued drift away from encryption toward data-theft-only extortion.

items.title: CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window.

items.title: Five federal agencies say attackers are mapping Siemens S7 controllers with AI-written tools dressed as monitoring software
items.content_text: NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August describing an active threat to Siemens S7 series programmable logic controllers in US critical infrastructure. The agencies say actors are using internet scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye to locate exposed or poorly protected S7 devices, then running AI-generated exploitation scripts presented as legitimate OT monitoring tools. The scripts are built on the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 libraries, which speak S7comm natively — so the traffic looks like ordinary engineering activity. Coverage spans the full line from S7-200 through the S7-1500 F-series safety controllers, and the agencies name critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture and commercial facilities as the most affected sectors. The assessed stage is reconnaissance and capability development, not confirmed manipulation.

items.title: A CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway, because the programming interface never asked who was calling
items.content_text: CISA’s advisory ICSA-26-237-03 covers a missing-authentication flaw in Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running versions up to and including 4.3.4.1. The device ships a Node-RED HTTP interface that does not enforce authentication, so an unauthenticated attacker who can reach it over the network can create flows that execute operating-system commands on the underlying host with maximum privileges. There is no exploit chain to assemble and no credential to guess; reachability is the whole vulnerability. Siemens rates it CVSS v3 10.0 and CISA lists the affected sectors as chemical, critical manufacturing, energy and transportation systems. The IoT2050 sits where these devices usually sit — on the seam between the plant network and whatever is collecting data from it — which means a compromised unit is a foothold with routes in both directions. No exploitation has been reported, but this is exactly the class of device the NSA/CISA joint advisory on internet-exposed industrial equipment has been describing, and the S7 activity in that advisory started with scanning for devices that answer.

items.title: CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04).

items.title: Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
items.content_text: Two days after a small UK generating station was reported to have run manually for four days following a cyberattack, the UK government tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope; the 24 August amendments add the supplier-designation instrument on top. The mechanism is adapted from the powers used against Huawei in 5G, with one reported difference practitioners have picked up on quickly: the requirement to publicly designate a vendor, and to serve the vendor a copy of the order, is reported as absent. Nothing is in force yet — the powers arrive on Royal Assent, and no date has been confirmed.
tags: Policy — UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill; supplier designation powers

items.title: In nine days, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process.

items.title: Maritime cyber gets a single owner in Washington — and, before long, a single enforcement strategy
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has established an Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG‑MCP), created under the Director of Inspections and Compliance as the service’s central authority for the cyber safety and security of the Marine Transportation System. Its remit is broader than it first sounds: domestic policy development, contribution to international standards, a coordinated compliance and enforcement strategy, and primary liaison with industry, other agencies, academia and the national laboratories. Rear Adm. Robert C. Compher framed it as keeping pace with a maritime industry whose growing use of information and operational technology brings efficiency and risk in the same package. The context matters as much as the announcement — it arrives roughly eighteen months after a GAO report found the Coast Guard could not readily produce complete data on cyber deficiencies found during vessel and facility inspections, and that its cyber strategy lacked risk assessment, performance measures and clear division of responsibilities. The Coast Guard has not said the new office was a direct response.

items.title: A national emergency over foreign grid equipment — and it reaches the firmware, not just the transformer
items.content_text: On 26 August the President signed Executive Order 14420, declaring a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act with respect to foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. The order covers high-voltage infrastructure at or above 69 kV — transformers, inverters, generators and battery energy storage — and explicitly extends to associated software, firmware and remote-access capability. It prohibits transactions initiated after 26 August involving acquisition, importation, transfer or installation of covered equipment tied to designated foreign entities where the transaction poses a sabotage or disruption risk, and directs the Department of Energy to issue implementing rules within 120 days. Those rules may condition the continued operation of equipment already energised, and potentially require removal. For utilities this becomes a supply-chain compliance layer on top of NERC CIP-013, and it lands on a provenance record most operators do not have.

items.title: Six agencies just told service providers how to communicate through an OT outage — and the plan has to survive losing your own systems
items.content_text: On 2 September CISA published Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers jointly with the FBI, Australia’s ACSC, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, NCSC‑UK and NCSC‑NZ. It is deliberately cause-agnostic — a cyberattack, an operator error, a failed switchgear and a storm all produce the same communication problem — and it asks providers to hold an incident communications plan with pre-agreed trigger thresholds and named audiences, to publish plain-language updates that state what is known and what is not, to give downstream customers root-cause and technical detail they can actually act on, and to keep all of it inside legal, regulatory, law-enforcement and containment constraints. For OT operators the relevance runs both directions: you are the downstream customer when an integrator, a cloud historian or a telemetry carrier goes dark, and you are the provider when a municipality, a regulator or a plant’s neighbours want to know why pressure dropped.
tags: Joint guidance — CISA, FBI, ACSC, CCCS, NCSC‑UK, NCSC‑NZ, service outage communications
